consensus_summary: The 'new moon' refers to the start of the biblical lunar month (astronomically understood as the dark conjunction or first visible crescent), which functions symbolically as a ceremonial shadow fulfilled in Christ, or as a motif for cyclical renewal and sacred time.
book_summary: The 'new moon' that marks the start of the month is astronomically the full moon in the east gate, serving as the sign of the appointed times, explicitly contrary to the common teaching that it is the dark conjunction or crescent.
consensus_core_identification: The start of the lunar month (dark/crescent moon) as a ceremonial shadow or symbol of renewal.
book_core_identification: The full moon in the east gate as the true marker for the start of the month.
boundary_disagreement: The book completely reassigns the astronomical referent of the 'new moon' from the dark/crescent phase to the full moon phase.
material_contradiction: The consensus accepts the traditional definition of the new moon as the dark conjunction or first visible crescent, while the book insists the biblical 'new moon' is actually the full moon.
rationale: The book explicitly rejects the commonly accepted astronomical definition of the new moon (first crescent/dark moon) and redefines it as the full moon, which is a material contradiction of the consensus understanding of what the symbol refers to in physical reality.
strongest_objection: Hebrew lexicography and historical Near Eastern calendars distinguish between the new moon ('chodesh', the renewed crescent) and the full moon ('keseh'). Interpreting the 'new moon' as the full moon contradicts both linguistic evidence and the established lunar-solar calendrical practices of ancient Israel.
